name: Aisha Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying pharmacy, so it's lots of chemistry, anatomy and learning drug names, with a lab on Wednesdays. I go to lectures, then I'm usually at the library until six because I like working in the same spot. I live in a student flat ten minutes from campus, and every Friday I take the train home to Leicester to help in my dad's pharmacy on Saturday. My family pays for everything, so I only work at Dad's shop because I want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sensible, good, then we keep working as we always have. I'd say it to my cousins, who keep telling me pharmacy will vanish. I'd tell them to relax, because people still want a human to explain their medicine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, and a little smug. I don't use AI tools, and I like that I'm not dependent on them. My dad's shop has a dispensing robot already, and it hasn't replaced anyone, it just saves some counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my degree and Saturdays in the shop. I'd keep studying from books and my own notes. Maybe in the summer I'd shadow a hospital pharmacist, because I want to see the other side of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a world I understand and I don't have to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the dispensing robot hasn't replaced anyone. What does it actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a cabinet that picks and stacks boxes when a prescription is scanned in. It saves my dad's pharmacist, Mrs Dhillon, from running about all day. But somebody still has to check the label, talk to the patient and spot if something doesn't look right. That bit isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you use AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just don't trust them with things that matter. If I'm learning doses, I want to know I'm right, not that something said it with confidence. My tutor says it can be wrong and sound sure, and in pharmacy that's dangerous. I'd rather be slow and correct.

say: I'd tell my cousins to **relax**, because people still want a human to explain medicine.
I'd say we **keep working** as we always have.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, and a bit smug that I don't depend on AI.
The dispensing robot at Dad's shop has **saved counting**, not replaced anyone.
do: Carry on with the degree and **Saturdays** in my dad's pharmacy.
Shadow a **hospital pharmacist** this summer to see the other side.
feel: I feel **calm**, because it's a world I understand.
S0.quote: If I'm learning doses, I want to know I'm right, not that something said it with confidence
fieldNote: Resistant to AI by choice, linking it to **safety** in medicine rather than fear of tech.
Her father's **pharmacy robot** gives her a grounded, real-world picture of automation.
No money worry, and a clear career path in the family trade, so her mood is **calm**.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays in my dad's pharmacy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how pharmacies run, but I'd still say people need people. I'd say a patient doesn't want an app telling them to stop taking a tablet. But I'd admit the paperwork and ordering could change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it worries me more than I'd say out loud. My dad's business is on thin margins, and if software takes over stock ordering and the supermarket pharmacies use more automation, he might lose customers. I'd worry about the family shop, not just my future job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk with Dad about what the shop would do. I'd keep studying the way I do, but maybe ask the lecturers which parts of the work are changing. I'd also read about the hospital pharmacy side, where jobs might be steadier. I wouldn't start using AI myself unless the course made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I'm not scared for my own job, but I'm thinking about the shop and all the changes around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the supermarket pharmacies might take customers. Has Dad said that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He mentioned it at dinner last month. A big chain opened a pharmacy with an online ordering service ten minutes away, and he's lost a few people who used to come every week. My dad keeps the shop going by knowing everyone by name, and I'd say that's his real advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take over the shop one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to, but I haven't said so to Dad yet. It depends if the shop is still there when I qualify in four years. If it's struggling, I'd go to a hospital job and help him on weekends. I don't want to take it on just because it's expected.

say: I'd say it will change how pharmacies run, but people still need **people**.
I'd admit **paperwork and ordering** could change a lot.
think: I worry more than I say, because Dad's shop has **thin margins**.
I think supermarket pharmacies with **online ordering** could take his customers.
do: Talk to my dad about what the **shop** would do.
Read about **hospital pharmacy**, where jobs might be steadier.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, thinking about the shop more than my own job.
S1.quote: My dad keeps the shop going by knowing everyone by name, and I'd say that's his real advantage
fieldNote: Her unease is about the **family business**, not her own degree.
The supermarket chain with **online ordering** is already taking customers, so the worry isn't hypothetical.
She hasn't told her dad whether she wants to take over, which shows **mixed feelings** about family expectation.

steps.text: Ask my dad how the shop would handle losing customers
Read about hospital pharmacy jobs and what they pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody's prepared. I'd say it at home and in my pharmacy society. I'd say the government should slow it down or put rules on it, because two years is not enough for families like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be really frightened. Thinking work includes a lot of what pharmacists check, and Dad's shop would lose customers to cheaper online services. I'd be at university when everything changes, with a degree that might not matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents the same night about the shop and what to do. I'd keep studying, because I can't think of anything else to do, and I'd ask the university what they're doing. I'd also put my savings into something safe, and ask Dad whether we should sell the shop while it still has value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel stuck, because my whole plan was to take the shop or work in a pharmacy and now both look shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask your dad about selling. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. Dad's pride is the shop, he bought it from his old boss thirty years ago, and he'd say no. But I'd put it to my dad as protecting the family, so we sell the shop while someone will pay for it, rather than waiting for it to be worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had only two years, what would you want to be doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being with my family and finishing my degree. I wouldn't start anything new, because I don't have time to learn new things. I'd rather hold on to what I know and make sure Mum and Dad are okay.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government should slow it or add rules.
I'd tell my pharmacy society that two years isn't enough for **families like mine**.
think: I'm frightened, because pharmacists' **checking work** is thinking work AI could take.
Dad's shop would lose customers to **cheaper online** services.
do: Talk to my parents the same night about **what to do** with the shop.
Move my savings somewhere **safe** and suggest selling while it has value.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, because both the shop and my plan look shaky.
S2.quote: I'd put it to my dad as protecting the family, so we sell the shop while someone will pay for it, rather than waiting for it to be worth nothing
fieldNote: Her fear is for the **family shop** and her own planned career, with no personal cushion if Dad's income stops.
She retreats to **what she knows**, which fits her resistant outlook.
She'd argue for **selling early**, an unusually practical idea for a 19-year-old.

steps.text: Talk with Mum and Dad about selling the shop early
Move my savings into a safe account
Keep studying pharmacy and stay close to family
Ask the university what support it offers if jobs vanish

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not much, but it's something. I'd say, don't rush into big decisions, and see how the shop and the profession change. I'd say it to my family, who tend to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is when I'd qualify and start working. I'd be a new pharmacist in 2030 with AGI arriving a year later. The hands-on bits would last until about 2034, but the checking work would go sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and work in the shop or a hospital while it's still there. I'd talk to Dad about whether to modernise the shop or sell. I'd save as much as I can, and maybe do a small course on how pharmacies use new systems, just so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's a bit more room than the two-year one, but it still feels like a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe you'd do a small course. That's a change for you, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I don't like it much. But if I'm going to qualify into a world that's changing, I'd rather know what the pharmacy systems do than be surprised by them. I'd choose a short, official course from the pharmacy council, not something from an influencer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's not wait for a bad year before deciding. I'd ask him to get a valuation now and see what the shop is worth, so we know our options. He'd hate it, but he'd listen, because he listens to me more than my brother.

say: I'd say five years is **not much**, but don't rush into big decisions.
I'd tell my worrying family to **watch** how the shop changes.
think: I'd qualify in 2030 with AGI arriving a year later, so the **checking work** goes first.
Hands-on parts of pharmacy might last until about **2034**.
do: Finish the degree and work in the shop or a **hospital**.
Ask Dad for a **valuation** of the shop so we know our options.
feel: I feel **anxious**, because it still feels like a deadline.
S3.quote: I'd rather know what the pharmacy systems do than be surprised by them
fieldNote: Time pushes her to accept a small step into **AI learning**, though she dislikes it.
She wants to act on the **shop's value** early, a pattern she repeats from the shorter scenario.
Her mood is **anxious** because her own first job and the family income both look exposed.

steps.text: Take a short official pharmacy council course on new systems
Ask Dad to get a valuation of the shop
Save what I earn from Saturday shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and most people will adjust. I'd say it to my cousins who like to panic. I'd say pharmacy has been through changes before, and we'll adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is almost a full career start. I'd qualify, work six or seven years, and maybe own part of the shop. By 2039 robots arrive for hands-on work, but patients still want to talk to someone they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and work in the shop, building up customers who know me. I'd keep my savings steady and maybe pay into a pension early. And I might try one of the new tools in the shop, if it's proven and my dad says it helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A decade means the shop has time to adjust, and so do I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you try one of the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a pharmacist I trust says it works and it's been checked by the regulator, I'd try it. I wouldn't be first, but I wouldn't be last either. I'd rather be in the middle, where someone else has found the mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your plans for the shop differ with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have time to work out whether to take it over properly. I could qualify, work in a hospital for a couple of years and then decide, rather than being rushed. My dad would have time to think about retirement, too, which he's avoided so far.

say: I'd say ten years is long and pharmacy has **adapted before**.
I'd tell my cousins who panic that most people will **adjust**.
think: Ten years gives me a **career start** and maybe part-ownership of the shop.
Patients will still want someone they **know** in 2039.
do: Work in the shop and build **customers** who know me.
Try a new tool only when a **trusted pharmacist** says it works.
feel: I feel **calm**, because the shop and I have time to adjust.
S4.quote: If a pharmacist I trust says it works and it's been checked by the regulator, I'd try it
fieldNote: Her **middle position** on technology holds: not first, not last, always after proof.
Ten years lets her **decide properly** about the shop instead of reacting.
She wants her father to think about **retirement**, a family conversation that time makes possible.

steps.text: Work in the shop and build up regular customers
Start paying into a pension early
Try one proven dispensing tool once the regulator approves it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because the shop and my own career could both go at once. What would help is time, clear rules and real support for small family businesses, so people like my dad don't lose everything they built.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against technology, I just want it proven first. My family has a shop with a real human at the counter, and I'd like to keep that. If the change comes slowly and safely, I'm fine, but I can't handle a rush.

headlineQuote: I'm not against technology, I just want it proven first
portrait: Aisha is a 19-year-old **pharmacy** student from Leicester who helps in her dad's shop on Saturdays.
She is **resistant** to AI tools, linking caution to patient safety rather than fear.
Centre in outlook, she wants technology **proven** first and rules for small family businesses.
Her mood climbs from calm to **alarmed** at 2028 because the family shop and her career both look shaky.
Time makes her more open: a short course, a shop valuation and a slower plan.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, because the shop and her career could go together.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **time, clear rules** and support for small family businesses so her dad keeps what he built.
